opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it as roughly a pyramid. At the base you have the huge pool of web-scale data: billions of image–text pairs scraped from the internet. It's noisy, captions are often wrong or unrelated, and aesthetic quality is all over the place, but it gives the model breadth. That's where it learns what the world looks like, a huge vocabulary of concepts, objects, and styles, and how language roughly maps onto visual content. You can't really get that coverage any other way.

The middle tier is filtered and curated data. You take that big pool and run classifiers on it for aesthetics, resolution, watermarks, safety, and image–text alignment. A lot of people now also recaption with a strong vision-language model, because the original alt-text is often terrible. You end up with a much smaller set, maybe an order of magnitude smaller, that's cleaner and better aligned. Training more on that tier improves prompt following and overall image quality noticeably.

At the top is the really small, high-quality tier: carefully selected or even commissioned images, sometimes human-rated, sometimes paired with preference data. It might be thousands or tens of thousands of examples rather than billions. You use it at the end, in a fine-tuning or alignment stage, and it has an outsized effect on the look of the model: composition, lighting, that polished quality people notice right away. What's interesting is how little of it you need, as long as the base model has already learned the breadth from the lower tiers.

So the way I'd put it is that the bottom tier teaches the model what's possible, and the top tier teaches it what's good. The tricky part is balancing them. If you over-fit to the top tier, you can lose diversity and the model starts producing the same kind of image for everything. If you lean too much on the bottom tier, you get breadth but the outputs look mediocre. A lot of the craft is in managing that transition, and also in being thoughtful about where the data comes from: licensing, consent, and what biases you're carrying along from the web.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts billions of noisy web-scale image–text pairs with a much smaller top tier of carefully selected or commissioned high-quality images.

r002.rationale: It describes the top-tier data as carefully selected or commissioned and scarce, but does not say that obtaining it is difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I tend to think of it as a pyramid, and the way the tiers stack up is really about the trade-off between quantity and quality, or maybe more precisely, between scale and control.

At the bottom you have the huge web-scraped datasets, the LAION-style stuff, billions of image-text pairs. The captions are noisy, the images are noisy, there's a lot of junk, duplicates, watermarks, stock photo text. But what that tier gives you is coverage. It's where the model learns what the visual world looks like, the long tail of objects and styles and compositions that you'd never think to collect deliberately. You don't get that breadth any other way.

Then the middle tier is what I'd call curated or filtered data. This is where you take that firehose and apply aesthetic scoring, resolution filters, dedup, caption quality filters, maybe recaptioning with a vision-language model so the text actually describes what's in the image. The images aren't fundamentally different from the bottom tier, but the signal-to-noise is a lot higher. And in practice this is where a lot of the real gains come from. People underestimate how much of model quality is just captions. If the model is trained on "IMG_2043.jpg" as the caption, it's not learning much about controllability.

And then at the top you have the small, high-quality, often licensed or human-annotated data. Professionally shot images, hand-written detailed captions, or data for specific capabilities like editing pairs, where you need a before and after that are precisely aligned. That tier is tiny by comparison, maybe thousands or tens of thousands of examples, but it's doing a disproportionate amount of work in terms of the final look and feel of the model. It's what you use for fine-tuning, for aligning toward what people actually consider a good image.

The thing I'd emphasize is that these tiers serve different purposes, and the mistake is to treat them as interchangeable. You can't fix a bad base with a beautiful fine-tuning set, because the model doesn't know enough about the world. And you can't get a polished, usable model from the raw web data alone, because it's learned every bad habit on the internet. So the question for us is usually less "which tier" and more "how do we sequence them and what are the right ratios," and that's honestly still more art than science.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts tiny high-quality datasets (thousands or tens of thousands of examples) with bottom-tier web-scraped data numbering billions of noisy image-text pairs.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the top-tier data is small and often licensed or human-annotated, but does not state that it is scarce because it is difficult to obtain.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a spectrum. At one end, you have very large amounts of image data from the web. It gives you broad coverage of what the world looks like, but the supervision is noisy. A caption might describe only one part of an image, or it might not really describe the image at all.

Then you have more curated data, where you’re paying attention to image quality, relevance, and how well the text matches the image. And then you have targeted data for a particular capability—carefully annotated examples, for instance, or human judgments about which outputs are better.

Those tiers serve different purposes. The broad data gives you coverage; the more curated and targeted data helps you shape the model’s behavior. So I wouldn’t think of it as simply replacing low-quality data with high-quality data. It’s about what signal you need at each stage of training.

r001.rationale: The response describes abundant web data and more curated tiers, but does not say that highly curated, high-quality data is limited in availability.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute any scarcity of curated data to difficulty obtaining it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a spectrum. At one end, you have large amounts of relatively uncurated data—images from the web with whatever text happens to be associated with them. That gives you broad coverage, but the signal can be pretty noisy. The text might describe the page rather than what’s actually in the image.

Then you have more curated data, where you’re filtering for quality and relevance and improving the captions. That can help the model learn a much stronger connection between the language and the visual content.

And then there’s very targeted data, potentially collected or annotated by people, that teaches a particular capability or captures human preferences. It’s more expensive, so you generally have less of it, but it can be especially useful for refining behavior.

The question isn’t just which tier is best. It’s how you combine that broad coverage with the more precise supervision, and where in training each kind of data is most useful.

r001.rationale: It contrasts large amounts of noisy, uncurated web data with much smaller amounts of targeted data that is collected or annotated by people.

r002.rationale: It says targeted data is potentially collected or annotated by people and is more expensive, which explains why less of it is available.
